questions.q: What does Page Life Expectancy (PLE) measure?
options: The average number of seconds a data page stays in the buffer pool before being evicted
The total number of currently connected sessions
The average time a query takes to compile
The number of transaction log backups taken per day
questions.explain: PLE is a Buffer Manager performance counter reflecting how long pages typically survive in memory before eviction.

questions.q: Where do you read Page Life Expectancy from?
options: sys.dm_os_performance_counters, filtered to the Buffer Manager object and the 'Page life expectancy' counter
sys.dm_os_wait_stats, filtered to wait_type = 'PLE'
sys.dm_exec_query_stats, ordered by total_worker_time
sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats, summed across all files
questions.explain: Despite sounding wait-related, PLE is a performance counter, exposed through sys.dm_os_performance_counters under the Buffer Manager object.

questions.q: Per this lesson, is the classic 'PLE below 300 seconds is bad' rule still reliable on modern servers?
options: No — it dates from small-RAM-era servers; PLE should be judged against buffer pool size and its own trend on that specific server, not one universal number
Yes — 300 seconds is still the single correct threshold for every server
No — PLE is meaningless and should never be checked
Yes — but only for servers with less than 1 TB of RAM
questions.explain: On a server with a large buffer pool, 300 seconds would mean the entire pool churns over every 5 minutes — far more severe than the old rule implied. A trend-based, size-relative read is more meaningful.

questions.q: What does a nonzero and growing RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE wait indicate?
options: Queries are queuing up waiting for a memory grant to become available, directly stalling their execution
The transaction log is being backed up
A network packet was dropped between client and server
The buffer pool has more memory than it needs
questions.explain: RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE accumulates when queries requesting memory grants (for sorts, hash joins, etc.) must queue because the memory-grant pool is contended.

questions.q: A server's PLE has been stable at 4,000 seconds for weeks, then drops to 800 seconds right after a new nightly reporting job is added, and stays there. What's the more useful interpretation per this lesson?
options: The sudden drop from a stable baseline is the meaningful signal worth investigating, regardless of whether 800 seconds alone would fail an old fixed threshold
800 seconds is comfortably above the old 300-second rule, so this can be ignored entirely
PLE readings are unreliable and should never be trusted after any workload change
This proves the buffer pool must be increased to exactly 5x its current size
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that a sudden drop from a stable baseline matters more than the absolute value — this pattern points at the new job changing the working set, worth investigating on its own terms.
